“More Chinese companies are put out of business by other Chinese companies. Chinese companies are not put out of business because of Western companies, so this whole competition is not, from a Chinese guy's mind, like a US-China competition. It’s more ‘how do I survive this gym?’ because it's damn hard to keep staying alive at home. That in turn makes you very competitive in the rest of the world.” Maura Fogarty speaks to Joe Ngai, Chairman of the China region for global consulting firm McKinsey. He advises senior management at Chinese and multinational corporations in the region which gives him a unique insight into the world’s second-largest economy. Having written numerous books and reports on China’s economic landscape, Ngai’s expertise has been recognised by accolades from the likes of Forbes China and Bloomberg. In this interview, we hear his thoughts about how the Chinese market has changed in the 25 years since the country joined the World Trade Organisation, and on how AI is developing and managing tensions with US competitors. Thank you to the Asia Business team for their help in making this programme. The Interview brings you conversations with people shaping our world, from all over the world. The best interviews from the BBC, including episodes with tech billionaire Reid Hoffman, director Chloé Zhao, and Dr Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, head of the World Trade Organisation. articles.title: Netflix is using an AI-generated Gene Wilder voice in its Willy Wonka reality show
articles.summary: Wonka’s The Golden Ticket will premiere September 23rd on Netflix, with Gene Wilder’s AI-recreated voice as part of the show.
articles.body: A new teaser trailer confirmed that Wonka’s The Golden Ticket will premiere on Netflix on September 23rd, following its Squid Game reality show in the trend of creating real competitions based on fictional torture scenarios. While the sets seen in the trailer are real and not some Glasgow-style AI fakes, the voiceover is AI-generated. Deadline reports that Netflix worked with AI audio company ElevenLabs with consent from Wilder’s family, after working on productions re-creating the voice of Michael Caine and Stan Lee. It also continues Netflix’s 2021 partnership with the Roald Dahl company, and is separate from the Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory animated feature that will arrive in 2027. As for the show itself, Netflix says its “high-stakes social experiment” will feature 12 “lucky” golden ticket winners plus their chosen partner in the competition, with one champion left standing a week later during the two-part finale on September 30th.

articles.title: ABC sues the FCC over Trump and Carr’s campaign of threats
articles.summary: ABC is suing the Federal Communications Commission over claims that the agency “waged a retaliatory campaign” against its networks over their political coverage.
articles.body: ABC is suing the Federal Communications Commission over claims the agency “waged a retaliatory campaign” against its networks over the content they broadcast. In a lawsuit filed in federal court on Tuesday, ABC and its parent company Disney accuse the FCC of “punishing ABC for its speech” by threatening its broadcast licenses. It’s the latest escalation in the dispute between ABC and the Trump administration, which has been critical of the network’s political coverage — especially by late-night host Jimmy Kimmel and The View. The FCC opened an investigation into The View’s airtime of political candidates in February and ordered ABC stations owned by Disney to file for an early license renewal in April. ABC fired back with a series of letters slamming the FCC’s decision, claiming it will chill free speech. It also didn’t broadcast President Donald Trump’s July 16th speech on its linear channels and streamed it on ABC News Live instead. ABC’s lawsuit alleges the Trump administration has “steadily increased the pressure” on its networks over the past several months, claiming the latest attack on its broadcast licenses “underscores the Commission’s true purpose: coercing and retaliating against a network that refuses to bow to the Administration’s demands.” Bloomberg reported in July that the FCC could take action against ABC and Disney as soon as this month. ABC and Disney are seeking a court order halting the FCC’s broadcast license renewal proceedings. In a statement to CNBC, an FCC spokesperson says, “Disney is obviously very concerned about the FCC’s proceeding, as evidenced by their ongoing campaign of disinformation as well as their decision to ask a court to stop the FCC from further pursuing matters.” The FCC will “continue to follow the facts and law wherever they lead,” the spokesperson adds. “The consequences of the Administration’s campaign against free speech reach well beyond ABC,” ABC’s lawsuit claims. “If the Administration gets its way, the message to every media company in the country will be unmistakable: tell only the stories the Administration deems favorable, or face the coercive machinery of the federal government. In such a world, the press could in no way be described as free.” Update, August 18th: Added a statement from the FCC.

articles.title: FBI raided Swalwell’s home, seized devices as part of sexual assault probe
articles.summary: Correction: The FBI raid of Swalwell’s home was related to sexual assault allegations. An earlier story included incorrect information. Updated at 12:18 p.m. EDT The FBI reportedly raided former Rep. Eric Swalwell’s (D-Calif.) home and confiscated his electronic devices over the weekend amid an ongoing probe, according to multiple outlets. The FBI searched the former congressman’s…
articles.body:
Correction: The FBI raid of Swalwell’s home was related to sexual assault allegations. An earlier story included incorrect information. Updated at 12:18 p.m. EDT

The FBI reportedly raided former Rep. Eric Swalwell’s (D-Calif.) home and confiscated his electronic devices over the weekend amid an ongoing probe , according to multiple outlets.

The FBI searched the former congressman’s home in Washington, D.C., Sunday after they seized devices from Swalwell in San Francisco on Saturday, per The New York Times. The probe concerns allegations of sexual assault, the newspaper reported.

The raid comes just days after news broke of Swalwell’s “physical relations” with Christine Fang, a suspected Chinese spy, as outlined in newly declassified documents released by the White House Government Transparency Task Force. The FBI had previously investigated Fang.

Allegations of sexual assault are ultimately what led Swalwell to suspend his campaign for California’s governorship and resign from his House seat in April. Swalwell has denied any wrongdoing.

Swalwell was accused of assaulting a Capitol Hill staffer — who was 17 years his junior — twice in the midst of his current marriage, as initially reported by the San Francisco Chronicle .

The former House Democrat is being investigated by the FBI, Manhattan district attorney’s office and the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department over the allegations that surfaced this spring.

In the Chinese spy probe, as revealed in the documents released earlier this week, Swalwell said he met Fang in 2015 and had “physical relations” with her on a “handful of occasions but never dated her or had a romantic relationship.”

Federal investigators determined she ran a political intelligence gathering operation directed by China’s primary civilian spy agency between 2011 and 2015.

An independent journalistic probe revealed that her objective was to infiltrate U.S. political circles to gather unclassified but sensitive political intelligence, manipulate campaign financing, and cultivate relationships with up-and-coming politicians who had national potential, as reported by Axios .

FBI memos show that Fang facilitated an illicit scheme to route campaign donations through straw donors.

In at least two cases, she used American conduits to obscure the fact that the political contributions were secretly being funded by the Chinese government.

Federal investigators also uncovered evidence that Fang placed Chinese nationals and foreign interns inside Swalwell’s congressional office in exchange for campaign fundraising support.

images.caption: Then-Rep. Eric Swalwell (D-Ca.), talks with reporters after holding a town hall meeting in Sacramento, Calif., on April 7, 2026.

articles.title: Twitch and Amazon face lawsuit over use of streamers' content to train AI
articles.summary: The lawsuit alleges Twitch used streamers' videos to train AI without their permission or proper compensation.
articles.body:
Amazon is facing a lawsuit over its move to train its AI models on videos people broadcast on the popular streaming platform Twitch.

The move faced backlash from users when it was announced in August - with people having the option to opt-out if they do not want their data used this way.

The class action lawsuit has been brought on behalf of millions of streamers who use Twitch, alleging its parent company Amazon used their videos to train AI without their permission or proper compensation.

Twitch and Amazon have not commented on the lawsuit.

Streamers on the platform reportedly produced more than 215 million hours of content in the first few months of 2026 alone.

The lawsuit was brought by Connecticut-based streamer Warren Pandiscia.

It claims Twitch breached its contract with users by using that content as AI training data for Amazon's models without obtaining their permission.

It adds streamers should not have their work commercially exploited to develop AI without consent or compensation.

The lawsuit seeks damages for streamers whose content was allegedly used to train AI, as well as an order preventing Amazon from continuing the alleged practice.

It is not clear when Amazon began collecting Twitch users' data to train its AI models.

Twitch's chief product officer Mike Minton previously said he did not know if users' data had been scraped for training before it gave people the opportunity to opt-out.

He said he was unsure what Amazon "has done in terms of model training and what they've used and not used".

In Twitch's own FAQs about AI training, it said a person's audio might be used to "refine models that create speech to text".

It said this would help improve automatic subtitles on Twitch streams as well as Amazon videos.

Those that want to disable the feature would need to navigate to the Settings tab in their Streamer Dashboard, click the Security and Privacy tab, then scroll down to near the bottom of the options and toggle off "training for Generative AI".

However, the opt-out only applies to individual streams, meaning creators' content could still be used for AI training when they appear in a stream where the feature remains enabled.

Amazon, which bought Twitch for nearly $1bn (£740m) in 2014, has made AI a major focus as it competes with Google, Meta and other tech giants.

articles.title: Netflix reportedly considers opening its app to other streamers
articles.summary: Executives discussed making Peacock and Fox One available through the Netflix app, The New York Times reports.
articles.body: Netflix executives have considered making third-party streaming services available within its app, according to a report from The New York Times. The recent discussions reportedly centered around bringing Peacock and Fox One to Netflix, though it’s unclear whether the streaming giant would sell subscriptions to the other services or add their content to its app. While Amazon’s Prime Video and Roku have long sold subscriptions to rival services, the move would be a major change for Netflix, which has only joined bundles with other streamers. YouTube — Netflix’s biggest rival — will also include access to Peacock as part of its Premium subscription next year. Netflix currently has no “imminent deal” planned, The New York Times reports. But Netflix has already begun dabbling in third-party streaming partnerships in France, where it folded live channels and streaming content from local broadcaster TF1 into its app in June. When asked about this partnership during a July earnings call, Netflix co-CEO Greg Peters said the company is seeing “promising” results. “If we see additional deals that similarly serve our members that work for our partner, that work for us, we’ll certainly consider them,” Peters said. Netflix declined to comment. Update, August 24th: Added Netflix’s response.

articles.title: ESPN streaming plans are getting more expensive
articles.summary: ESPN is raising prices across its plans, with the ad-supported Select tier going from $12.99 to $13.99 per month, and its Unlimited plan increasing from $29.99 to $31.99 per month.
articles.body: ESPN is hiking the price of its subscription on September 17th, a change that will also impact its bundles with Disney Plus. In a support page spotted earlier by Sports Media Watch, ESPN says its ad-supported Select membership will cost $13.99 instead of $12.99 / month, while its Unlimited plan will rise to $31.99 from $29.99 / month. The annual ESPN Select plan is also going to $139.99 from $129.99 / year, and the annual Unlimited tier is increasing to $319.99 from $299.99 / year. Meanwhile, Disney Plus bundles with ESPN Select are going up in price as well. Here’s a rundown of the changes: * Disney Plus (with ads), Hulu (with ads), and ESPN Select: $21.99 / month, up from $19.99 / month. * Disney Plus (ad-free), Hulu (ad-free), ESPN Select: $32.99 / month, up from $29.99. * Legacy Disney Plus (ad-free), Hulu (ad-free), and ESPN Select: $27.99 / month, up from $24.99 / month. Disney Plus bundles with ESPN Unlimited aren’t affected. Last week, Axios reported that about 80 percent of Unlimited subscribers signed up through the bundle with Disney Plus and Hulu. Though Disney last raised prices across its bundles last year, this is the first increase for ESPN, which rolled out its standalone streaming subscription last August. As part of the launch, ESPN updated its mobile app with a TikTok-like feed of videos and a personalized version of SportsCenter. ESPN also launched multiview in its app on major smart TV platforms.

articles.title: Amazon and Twitch Face Class-Action Lawsuit After Introducing Opt-Out Setting That Uses Streamers' Content to Train AI
articles.summary: Twitch and Amazon are facing a class-action lawsuit after the streaming platform rolled out a feature that automatically trains its generative AI on streamers’ content unless they opt out.
articles.body:
Twitch and Amazon are facing a class-action lawsuit after the streaming platform rolled out a feature that automatically trains its generative AI on streamers’ content unless they manually opt out.

The setting sparked a wave of backlash when it was rolled out last week. "Allow your channel content to train generative AI content models at Amazon," it reads.

It’s buried in users’ security and privacy settings, and is automatically turned on by default. Streamers must toggle the option off in order to opt out of it — but that doesn’t stop Twitch from using their channel content for other purposes, as outlined in the platform’s Privacy Notice .

We've added a setting that lets you opt out of having your channel content used to train generative AI content models across Amazon. Click here to learn more: — Twitch Support (@TwitchSupport) August 12, 2026

We've added a setting that lets you opt out of having your channel content used to train generative AI content models across Amazon. Click here to learn more:

Just a week later, Amazon and Twitch were officially named in a class-action lawsuit filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California on August 20, 2026. In the 37-page complaint, plaintiff Warren Pandiscia — a Twitch streamer based in Connecticut with over 900 followers — argues that Amazon “unlawfully” scraped creators’ content without their consent by automatically opting them into the AI training setting.

“Defendants’ actions were not only unlawful, but an unconscionable attack on the community of content creators whose content is used to fuel the multitrillion-dollar generative AI industry without any compensation," the suit reads.

"Content creators such as Plaintiff and the Class Members will never be able to claw back the intellectual property unlawfully copied and used by Defendants to train Amazon’s generative AI. Once AI ingests content, that content is stored in its neural network, and not capable of deletion or retraction. Defendants’ actions constitute abuse and exploitation of content creators’ work for Defendants’ profit."

Damages sought include “all available contract damages, including actual, compensatory, consequential, and nominal damages, together with such other relief as the Court deems just and proper,” though no specific monetary amount was mentioned.

Twitch, for its part, has defended its stance on automatically opting creators into Amazon’s AI training. During a ‘Patch Notes’ stream that was broadcast that same day, Twitch's chief product officer Mike Minton responded to questions about the setting, saying plainly: “If it was opt-in, nobody would opt in. That’s honestly the answer.”

Twitch’s Account Settings FAQ explains that it trains Amazon’s generative AI on users’ content for things like “[refining] models that create speech to text, which would help improve captions at Twitch but would also help improve captions across Amazon,” and “AI-supported features, like captions, which automatically generate captions for your Clips but does not retain your stream or your clips to train a model that can generate new content.”

Twitch has not provided an official comment on the lawsuit at the time of writing. IGN has reached out for comment.

Image Credit: Wesley Tingey, Unsplash.com

Virginia (she/her) is IGN’s News Editor. With ten years of experience reporting on games and entertainment, she’s got a storied background in the fighting game community, influencer news, and viral online trends. Find her on Twitter at @TheeMissGlaze .

articles.title: Democrat rips Hasan Piker as 'hack who thrives on hate' over his warning to American Jews about Israel
articles.summary: Rep. Hillary Scholten condemned Hasan Piker's remarks about American Jews and Israel, calling the Twitch streamer a "hack who thrives on hate."
articles.body: Controversial far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who has become increasingly prominent in Democratic politics, is facing backlash from Rep. Hillary Scholten, D-Mich., over his remarks about American Jews' support for Israel that she characterized as "talk of violence" targeting Jewish Michigan state Sen. Jeremy Moss. In a statement published Monday, Scholten said Piker was "a hack who thrives on hate, shock and awe because he lacks substance." "Hasan Piker's talk of violence against American Jews, and directly naming a Michigan elected official, and future member of Congress, Jeremy Moss, is unacceptable. Full stop," Scholten's statement read. "We should all be calling out this disgusting rhetoric so it loses its grip on our politics once and for all. It has no place in Michigan, and no place in our country." HASAN PIKER IS BECOMING THE 'FACE OF THE PROGRESSIVE MOVEMENT,' FORMER DEMOCRATIC OPERATIVE WARNS In his response to Scholten's statement, Piker called Scholten an "Israel 1st congresswoman." "if i was an israel 1st congresswoman with a possible cheating scandal with a republican in the state, i wouldn’t spend so much time vying for the spotlight by actively defaming a prominent antizionist voice to harm the dem senate majority chances over a 90/10 issue," Piker wrote on X. Piker, who holds a large social media following, has been particularly visible in Michigan this election cycle. He backed Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated Rep. Haley Stevens in a primary earlier this month. El-Sayed was criticized for appearing with Piker during his campaign, with some saying that the streamer's rhetoric was too extreme. Scholten backed Stevens last month, calling her a "smart, capable, and common-sense leader." She later praised Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer for endorsing Stevens. El-Sayed also responded to Piker's comments, and while he did not condemn the streamer outright, he denounced antisemitism and rhetoric that puts the Jewish community in danger. "I believe all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence. This is particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past," El-Sayed wrote. "My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters," he added. "Antisemitism is a scourge, and we need to address it in all its forms. And I stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk." EL-SAYED DISAVOWS HASAN PIKER'S 9/11 COMMENTS BUT DECRIES 'CANCEL CULTURE' In his statement, El-Sayed stressed that Piker did not speak for his campaign, writing that, "nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople." In addition to politicians, Piker was also criticized by Jewish organizations.  In a statement to Fox News Digital, the Jewish Federation of Detroit said that "Hasan Piker’s talk of violence against Jewish Americans while displaying a picture of a Michigan lawmaker who is Jewish is repugnant and antisemitic." "We call on all responsible leaders to condemn this extremist, attention-seeking conduct which divides Americans, foments hate, and makes our Jewish community less safe," the Jewish Federation of Detroit's statement read. The American Jewish Committee (AJC) also said on Monday that by using an image of Moss, "Piker put a target on the backs of Sen. Moss, Jewish candidates and officeholders, and American Jews alike." "Blaming Jews for the antisemitism directed at them is itself antisemitism," AJC wrote on X. "Every public official who has shared his platform now has a choice: denounce this and walk away, or be complicit. There is no third option." Anti-Defamation League CEO Jonathan Greenblatt weighed in as well, questioning whether elected officials who associate with Piker really watch his streams or if "they just see his reach and ignore the rampant antisemitism." "The Jewsplaining is extraordinary: Piker appoints himself an authority on antisemitism, lecturing Jews about what is and isn’t antisemitic while blaming the Jewish community for the hatred directed against it," Greenblatt said of Piker. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE During his Aug. 20 stream, Piker seemed to warn American Jews against supporting Israel, saying that doing so could lead to violence against them. "People don't f--- with Israel any longer. And if Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they're singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone will come around and take action not against Israel, mind you, but against American Jews," Piker said. When he made the comment, Piker had an image of Moss, who is running to fill Stevens' seat, in his background. Piker's remarks came amid a controversy over an audio clip circulating online in which Moss purportedly said that the "entire purpose" of his congressional campaign was to ensure America's continued support for Israel. However, the Michigan Democrat said that the clip was fabricated, calling it "a manipulated and unsourced audio, with things I never did and never would say." "We are in a dangerous era of disinformation. Circulating a lie because it affirms your bias or belief is equally bad whether it comes from the left or the right. We all have a choice not to spread fabricated images, videos, and audio about candidates and campaigns. We all have a role in stopping the erosion of our democracy," Moss said about the controversy over the audio clip. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to Piker and Moss for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

articles.body: It's nearly here. The moment Wall Street waits for every quarter since the AI trade kicked off: Nvidia's (NVDA) second quarter earnings.Yes, while its Big Tech peers reported their results nearly a month ago, Nvidia is finally giving us the lowdown on its latest quarter when it reports Q2 earnings after the close on Wednesday.For the quarter, Nvidia is expected to report second quarter adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $2.09 on revenue of $92 billion, according to Bloomberg analyst consensus estimates. articles.title: Instagram’s ‘First Draft’ trims your Reels clips for you
articles.summary: Instagram is rolling out a new Reels-editing feature that automatically trims your clips to make them ready to share.
articles.body: Instagram is launching a new Reels-editing feature that automatically trims your video clips to focus on the highlights. The feature, called First Draft, is rolling out to Instagram’s iPhone app and provides a “starting point” that you can build upon with other edits, according to an announcement on Tuesday. An example shared by Instagram shows a user selecting multiple clips for a reel and then tapping the “First Draft” button. From there, Instagram analyzes the clips — each of which is more than a minute long — before trimming them down to eliminate pauses and showcase the most important parts. Instagram then combines the snippets into a reel that’s ready to edit and share. [Video: Instagram First Draft] It sounds similar to Adobe’s AI-powered Quick Cut feature, which automatically combines clips based on a prompt. But unlike Adobe’s feature, Instagram’s First Draft tool doesn’t use AI, according to Instagram spokesperson Nicole Rechtszaid. Instagram says First Draft works with “multi-clip montages, talking-head videos, and day-in-the-life content.” You can find the feature by opening the camera app in Instagram, filming your video, and tapping the First Draft Button. You can also find it in your Reels gallery after selecting more than one clip. Update, August 25th: Added confirmation that First Draft doesn’t use AI.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed distances from Hasan Piker — kind of
articles.summary: Is Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed distancing himself from controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker? That’s the headline, but it’s not quite true.
articles.body:
Is Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed distancing himself from controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker? That’s the headline, but it’s not quite true. I’d say it’s a tepid distancing at best. Itty bitty distancing.

First, Hasan Piker made some truly awful (but entirely characteristic) comments about how Jewish people are really sort of just asking for it with those whole supporting Israel thing — sooner or later, somebody’s going to do something bad to the Jews because they like Israel. Seriously, that’s the gist of what he said .

Now, those comments were specifically aimed at Jeremy Moss, a Michigan state senator and Democrat who has been reluctant to endorse El-Sayed due to his proximity to the relentless Israel critic. And they’re truly vile sentiments. In the first place, likening the state of Israel to ISIS is simply ridiculous. Again, for the thousandth time, it’s fine to criticize Israel or disagree with its government or think that it’s caused too much destruction in Gaza. But you’re living in a delusion if you think Israel is like ISIS only Jewish.

Piker is living in that delusion though, and he thinks it’s so obvious that Israel is ISIS levels of bad that someone, I guess, is going to come along and hurt Jewish people unless they really turn on Israel.

I should note that this is already happening: There is rising antisemitism on both the left and the right and, yes, it’s partly because Israel’s popularity has declined. It’s one thing to recognize that fact, and it’s quite another to imply — as Hasan Piker assuredly did — that the Jews basically deserve it unless they disassociate from Israel entirely. It’s basically very similar to the discourse around America deserving 9/11 , one of Piker’s earlier controversial remarks.

But Piker was also directing this comment at Moss very significantly, including by sharing a picture of him. What he’s implying is, denounce Israel or else who knows what’s going to happen. Something very bad.

And he’s been called out for it by Democrats, including Rep. Hillary Scholten .

Scholten has also been reluctant to endorse El-Sayed. So El-Sayed, who campaigned alongside Piker and chose him to be a surrogate and spokesperson, is finally speaking up — sort of. El-Sayed put out a statement that he claimed was aimed at Piker’s comments about Moss, although he doesn’t mention either of them in the statement. He writes:

“I believe all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence. This is particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past. My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters. Antisemitism is a scourge, and we need to address it in all its forms. And I stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk. But I want to be crystal clear, nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople.”

OK, but El-Sayed clearly tried to cash in on Piker’s star power by associating with him. If he now wants to disassociate, he’s got to say it more explicitly than that.

What’s really happening is that El-Sayed can read polling data, and he’s concerned he could actually blow this race, even in a political environment that’s maximally unfriendly for Republicans. So he’s distancing himself ever so slightly.

Of course, I suspect El-Sayed might actually agree with the spirit of what Piker said. In fact, when Temple Israel in West Bloomfield, Mich., was attacked by a deranged man, an Arab American who had lost family members in Lebanon, El-Sayed said repeatedly, “hurt people hurt people.”

That’s probably why some Jewish Michiganders are having trouble supporting him. Because they don’t see a tremendous amount of distance between Hasan Piker and Abdul El-Sayed.

And some Democrats understand that this is a problem, even very progressive ones. Activist Cameron Kasky wrote on X : “Hasan Piker is absolutely a ‘problem’ for Democrats. Centrists are attacking our party over him instead of the authoritarianism and corruption unfolding literally right before our eyes.

“Republicans are laughing about it,” he continues. “We are fabricating an electoral weakness out of thin air.”

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: Tech stocks today: Meta agrees to settle social media case for $16.68 billion
articles.body: Meta (META) agreed to settle a social media addiction case with a group of state attorneys general on Wednesday, putting an end to the trial in its second week. The stock initially popped on the news before paring gains.The case revolved around allegations from 29 states that Instagram and Facebook developed products to hook young users on the platforms and harvested the data of children under 13 to their benefit.According to court filings, Meta denied wrongdoing and agreed to pay up to $16.68 billion.In a statement on the company's website, Meta said, "Ensuring teens have a safe and productive experience on our platforms is an absolute imperative for Meta. We want to get this right for parents and teens, and that's why we partnered with state attorneys general to set a new industry standard."According to DC Attorney General Brian L. Schwalb, these are among the safety features Meta has agreed to implement:Hard cap daily time limits and "Productive Pauses" for children on its two platforms, Instagram and Facebook. Meta will adopt a combined two-hour daily time limit with mandatory pauses after 15 minutes of continuous use and again at 60 and 90 minutes to interrupt endless scrolling. These limits remain in effect for five years. If Snapchat, TikTok, and YouTube adopt comparable terms, the daily limit on each platform will drop to 60 minutes for 10 years."Nighttime blocks" restricting children's access to feeds from 12:00 a.m. to 6:00 a.m and silencing notifications from 10:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m.Limited school-time access for children, eliminating push notifications on weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. during the school year.Strict age verification measures and safer, age-appropriate content controls, including stronger safeguards against bullying, content promoting eating disorders, and content related to suicide and self-harm.Stronger, more user-friendly parental controls.Limits on social comparison features, including beauty filters and visible "like" counts that have been linked to poor mental health outcomes for kids.Regular assessment by an independent auditor of the implementation and efficacy of the safety features, with oversight by the settling states.Nvidia earnings on tapMeta isn't the only tech giant making headlines. Another key moment for Wall Street is due to arrive after the bell on Wednesday: Nvidia's (NVDA) second quarter earnings.While its Big Tech peers reported their results nearly a month ago, Nvidia is finally giving us the lowdown on its latest quarter when it reports Q2 earnings after the close on Wednesday.For the quarter, Nvidia is expected to report second quarter adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $2.09 on revenue of $92 billion, according to Bloomberg analyst consensus estimates. That would mark a 96% year-over-year jump in overall revenue, and a continued quarter-over-quarter acceleration.
